body.hook: Before an actor says a single word, the audience already knows a lot about their character: whether they're confident or nervous, old or young, powerful or afraid. How? Through posture, levels and the way they move through space.

study.title: Status and Levels
study.question: How do levels and posture show who a character is?
study.passage:
Warm-up, Status walk (8 minutes): Walk around the room. The leader calls out numbers from 1 (very low status: shy, unsure) to 10 (very high status: confident, powerful). Change your posture, pace, eye contact and space with each number.
Activity 1, Levels tableau (10 minutes): In groups of four, create three tableaux using low, medium and high levels:
• A king and his servants
• A team celebrating a win while one player sits injured
• A new student arriving at a busy cafeteria
The audience guesses each character's status and explains the evidence.
Activity 2, Status card scene (15 minutes): In pairs, each person secretly draws a status card (1–10). Improvise a short scene in a setting such as a job interview, a bus stop or a restaurant. Show status only with posture, levels, eye contact and space, not by saying it. The audience guesses each number.
Debrief: Which physical choices showed status most clearly?
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.
steps: Warm up with the status walk
discussion: How did your posture change from status 1 to 10?
In the tableaux, how did levels show relationships?
Which physical clue was easiest for the audience to read?
Can a character change status during a scene? How?
study.product: Choose a character from a story or film and describe how you would show their status through posture, level, eye contact and use of space, with a sketch of a tableau.

body.hook: Before an actor says a word, the audience has already guessed their character from the way they walk into the room. A nervous teenager, a proud queen and a tired farmer each move completely differently.

study.title: Walk This Way
study.question: How can the body show who a character is?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Leading centres (10 minutes): Walk around the room leading with different body parts. Nose (curious, nosy), chest (proud, confident), forehead (thinking, intelligent), belly (relaxed, jolly), knees (tired, clumsy), hips (cool, carefree). What character does each suggest?
2. Tempo (5 minutes): Walk at tempo 1 (very slow) to 10 (frantic). Combine a centre and a tempo: chest at 3 = a calm king; nose at 9 = a nosy reporter.
3. Status walks (10 minutes): Walk as high status (head up, slow, takes space, eye contact) and low status (head down, quick, small steps, avoids eye contact).
4. Character cards (20 minutes): Each student draws a card (e.g., elderly gardener, nervous new student, famous chef, superhero in disguise). Create a walk, a signature gesture and a posture. Enter, cross the stage, do one action, and exit. Classmates guess the character.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; leading-centre work is a common actor-training exercise.

Create a character walk, gesture and posture
discussion: Which leading centre created the strongest character?

study.product: Perform a character entrance, action and exit using a chosen leading centre, tempo, status and signature gesture, and explain your choices.

body.objective: Students will be able to create a physical theatre piece.

successCriteria: I can create a short physical theatre piece

body.hook: Physical theatre companies like Frantic Assembly tell stories almost entirely with movement: bodies lift, fall, chase and freeze. No set, very few words, but audiences feel every moment.

vocabulary.definition: Theatre that tells stories mainly through movement.
A movement that is repeated with meaning.

study.title: Bodies Tell the Story
study.question: How can a group tell a story through movement alone?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
Safety first: Any contact must be agreed (consent), practised slowly, and stopped if anyone is uncomfortable. No lifts in this lesson.
1. Proxemics (10 minutes): In pairs, show relationships only through distance: best friends, strangers, enemies, a parent and child.
2. Counterbalance (5 minutes): Pairs hold hands and lean back slowly, then shoulder to shoulder. Communicate and come up together.
3. Motif (5 minutes): Create a movement that means something, e.g., a hand reaching out = hope. Repeat it three ways: fast, slow, with a partner.
4. Create (25 minutes): Groups of four create a 90-second piece on one theme: friendship, the first day at a new school, a storm, or waiting for news. Requirements: one motif repeated at least twice, three levels, one slow-motion moment, changing proxemics, a clear beginning and end. Music without lyrics may play.
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson; Frantic Assembly is a UK physical theatre company known for this approach.
steps: Build a 90-second movement piece on a theme
discussion: What does your motif mean, and how did it change?
Where did you use slow motion and why?
Could the audience understand your theme without words?
study.product: Perform a 90-second physical theatre piece with a repeated motif, three levels and a slow-motion moment, and explain the meaning of your motif.
